# Hard-to-vary report: Bostrom, "Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?"

## 1. The question, frozen

The title asks a yes/no question, but the abstract and opening make the real target a disjunction: at least one of (1) humanity almost certainly goes extinct before a "posthuman" stage, (2) posthuman civilizations almost never run many ancestor-simulations, (3) we are almost certainly in a simulation. I take the disjunction, plus its conditional rider (reject (1) and (2) and your credence in (3) should approach 1), as the frozen question, since that is what the argument actually delivers — the title over-promises against it. Range: any civilization that could reach "posthuman" computing capacity. Kind of question: mostly backward/identification (given population fractions and no distinguishing evidence, what credence should an observer assign?), not a causal "what produced this."

## 2. The explanation in parts

Substrate-independence (weak form); the numeric estimates of posthuman computing power; the algebraic derivation of the trilemma from Pf, fI, NI, H; the bland indifference principle; the argument distinguishing it from the Doomsday argument; the treatment of "me-simulations" versus full ancestor-simulations; the theological/hierarchy speculation in Section VI.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Also say |
|---|---|---|
| Substrate-independence | Borrowed | Rests on the functionalism/computationalism debate; Bostrom writes "we shall here take it as a given" — not defended here. Everything downstream is held only *if* this is true. |
| Numeric estimates (10^33–10^36 ops/ancestor-sim; 10^42 ops/sec) | Loose | The text itself says the conclusion survives being off by "several orders of magnitude." Swap the numbers, nothing moves. What's actually held is the qualitative claim that per-simulation cost is vast on posthuman scales. |
| Trilemma derivation (equation *) | Held | This is essentially algebra from the stated definitions of Pf, fI, NI, H, fsim. Remove it and the disjunction has no support. It is *built*, not asserted — a reader can rerun it. |
| Bland indifference principle | Borrowed | The fuller defense is explicitly deferred to another work ("space does not permit a recapitulation"). Here it gets only one analogy (junk DNA) and one negative argument (see below). |
| Doomsday-argument distinction | Held | Does real work: names a concrete difference (random-sample-across-all-time vs. no-information-about-which-observer-you-are) that blocks a specific, named rival objection. |
| Me-simulations vs. ancestor-simulations | Unknown | Bostrom flags that ~10^11 times as many me-simulations would be needed to dominate, and says outright "it is not clear" how much cheaper they'd be. This is an open boundary condition on the anthropic step, not a settled one. |
| Theological/hierarchy speculation (gods, afterlife, "virtuous circle") | Idle | Offered as "loose analogies." Remove the whole passage and the trilemma is untouched. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** If posthuman computing power turned out modest rather than vast, NI would not be "extremely large," and (*) would no longer force the disjunction — fsim could stay small even with Pf and fI not small. So the argument does not explain every possible outcome; it genuinely depends on the "immense computing power" premise. That's a point in its favor.

**Direction.** The indifference-principle step is careful to stay on the identification side ("what can we tell from what we see") rather than sliding into a production claim, and Section V spends real effort separating it from the Doomsday argument's different (and more contested) premise — a random sample across all time. That separation is itself a tested move, not just asserted.

**Answer hidden in the starting points?** Partly. "We have no information that our own experience is any more or less likely to be simulated" is the trigger for the indifference principle, but there is no stated gauge for what would count as such information. That makes this trigger condition function like a **catch-all** with no gauge: anyone could claim to have (or lack) "information that bears on which observer they are," and the argument has no independent check on which is so.

**Pairs that pull.** Bostrom notes the tension himself: vast, cheap computation pushes toward disjunct (3) being forced, while posthuman ethical sophistication is one route to disjunct (2) (a ban on ancestor-simulations). He doesn't resolve which wins — he reports it as an open pull, which is honest rather than hidden.

**Rivals.** Unusually, the argument's own structure supplies its strongest rivals: (1) and (2) *are* the rival explanations to (3), stated by the author rather than smuggled in or dismissed. That is a real strength against the "hunt the answer in the starting points" test.

**Where the parts came from.** A mix: the derivation is built; the numeric estimates are built from cited physical bounds but loose in exact value; substrate-independence and the full defense of the indifference principle are borrowed from elsewhere and only asserted here.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

- Give an explicit gauge for "no information that bears on which observer you are" — right now nothing would show this trigger condition is misfiring or being smuggled in.
- Say what happens to the whole apparatus if substrate-independence is false: does fsim become undefined, or does the trilemma just collapse to "no simulated minds exist, so no observers there," which is a different (and much weaker) argument?
- Bound the me-simulation/ancestor-simulation cost ratio. It's the one place the paper says "not clear," and it materially changes what a high credence in (3) would even mean (in a me-simulation vs. a full-history one).

## 6. What this does not show

That the trilemma's *derivation* is hard to vary (survives swapping the numbers, doesn't cover every outcome, isn't hidden in its own premises) does not show the conclusion is *true*. Two of its load-bearing parts — substrate-independence and the fuller defense of the bland indifference principle — are borrowed from elsewhere and only asserted or lightly defended in this document. A reader who rejects either premise is not thereby shown to have missed a flaw in the algebra; they are rejecting an import the paper itself flags as imported.

## 7. One next step

Run this same method on the bland indifference principle itself, using its fuller defense in Bostrom's *Anthropic Bias* (cited but not reproduced here), since that is the least-tested load-bearing part in this document and the one on which the credence-close-to-x step (#) most directly depends.
